videos.summary: Practical guide to using LLMs in daily work. Karpathy demonstrates ChatGPT settings, explains when to use different models (GPT-4 vs Claude vs Gemini), covers prompt engineering basics, and shows real workflows including coding, writing, and research tasks.
key_insights: GPT-4 is best for complex reasoning tasks but Claude excels at long-form writing
System prompts are the most underutilized feature for power users
The o1/o3 reasoning models are transformative for math and coding but overkill for simple tasks
videos.creator_stance: LLMs are powerful tools that require skill to use effectively — most people use them at only 10% of their potential. The key is learning when to use which model and how to structure prompts.
notable_quotes: I want to show you how I use these tools and how you can also use them in your own life and work

videos.summary: Comprehensive introduction to how LLMs work — from training data through tokenization, neural network architecture, and the psychology of how these models 'think'. Covers the full pipeline of building ChatGPT-class models.
key_insights: LLMs are fundamentally token predictors — understanding this explains most of their behaviors and failures
The 'stochastic parrot' debate misses that compression of internet-scale data requires genuine understanding
Sharp edges exist because models optimize for plausible next tokens, not truth
videos.creator_stance: LLMs are remarkable tools with genuine cognitive capabilities, but users need mental models for understanding their strengths and failure modes. They're not just autocomplete — but they're not AGI either.
notable_quotes: it is obviously magical and amazing in some respects it's really good at some things not very good at other things and there's also a lot of sharp edges to be aware of

videos.summary: Hands-on reproduction of GPT-2 (124M parameters) from scratch. Walks through the original OpenAI code, explains the architecture, and rebuilds it step by step in PyTorch, covering data loading, model definition, training loops, and evaluation.
key_insights: GPT-2's 124M model is small enough to reproduce on a single GPU in reasonable time
The original OpenAI code is surprisingly readable and well-structured
Understanding the architecture at code level demystifies what these models actually do
videos.creator_stance: The best way to understand LLMs is to build one from scratch. Reproducing GPT-2 is the ideal learning project — complex enough to be educational, simple enough to complete.
notable_quotes: when openai released gpt2 this was 2019 and they released it with this blog post on top of that they released this paper and on top of that they released this code on GitHub

videos.summary: Deep dive into tokenization — the least glamorous but most important preprocessing step in LLMs. Covers BPE algorithm, byte-level encoding, special tokens, and the many hidden failure modes caused by tokenization choices.
key_insights: Tokenization is Karpathy's 'least favorite part' but understanding it explains many LLM quirks
Many LLM failures (counting, spelling, non-English languages) trace directly back to tokenization
Byte-level BPE is elegant but creates uneven representation across languages
videos.creator_stance: Tokenization is the most underappreciated component of LLMs. Most users don't understand it, but it explains the majority of weird model behaviors.
notable_quotes: tokenization is my least favorite part of working with large language models

videos.summary: 30-minute accessible talk on what LLMs are, how they work, and why they matter. Covers the key concepts — that an LLM is essentially two files (parameters + code), the training process, and emergent capabilities.
key_insights: An LLM is fundamentally just two files — the parameters and the code to run them
LLaMA 2 70B represents the state of the art in open-weight models
The jump from smaller to larger models isn't just quantitative — capabilities emerge qualitatively
videos.creator_stance: Everyone should understand the basics of how LLMs work. The 'two files' mental model is the simplest way to grasp what these systems are.

videos.summary: Deep dive into tokenization — the least glamorous but most important preprocessing step in LLMs. Covers BPE algorithm, byte-level encoding, special tokens, and the many hidden failure modes caused by tokenization choices.
key_insights: Tokenization is Karpathy's 'least favorite part' but understanding it explains many LLM quirks
Many LLM failures (counting, spelling, non-English languages) trace directly back to tokenization
Byte-level BPE is elegant but creates uneven representation across languages
videos.creator_stance: Tokenization is the most underappreciated component of LLMs. Most users don't understand it, but it explains the majority of weird model behaviors — from inability to count letters to poor non-English performance.
notable_quotes: tokenization is my least favorite part of working with large language models but unfortunately it is necessary to understand in some detail because it is fairly hairy gnarly

videos.summary: Fifth installment of the makemore series, upgrading from MLP to WaveNet-style architecture for character-level language modeling. Demonstrates hierarchical processing and dilated convolutions for better context handling.
key_insights: Moving from 3-character to longer context windows dramatically improves generation quality
WaveNet's hierarchical structure processes information at multiple time scales
The progression from MLP → RNN → WaveNet shows the evolution of sequence modeling thinking
videos.creator_stance: Complexifying architectures incrementally — starting simple and adding complexity — is the right way to learn deep learning. Each upgrade teaches a fundamental concept.
notable_quotes: we would like to take more characters in a sequence as an input not just three

videos.summary: Manual backpropagation through the MLP language model to deeply understand gradient flow. Implements backward passes by hand before using PyTorch autograd, revealing the mechanics of neural network training.
key_insights: Implementing backprop by hand reveals that it's just the chain rule applied systematically
Most deep learning bugs are in the backward pass — understanding it helps debug
PyTorch autograd is elegant but understanding the manual version builds real intuition
videos.creator_stance: Everyone rushes to the exciting architectures, but understanding backpropagation at a deep level is what separates practitioners from cargo-culters. One more lecture on MLPs is worth it.

videos.summary: Analyzing activation statistics and gradient flow during neural network training. Introduces batch normalization, explains initialization schemes, and diagnoses common training pathologies.
key_insights: Monitoring activation distributions during training reveals problems before loss curves do
Batch normalization was revolutionary because it stabilized gradient flow
Proper initialization (Kaiming, Xavier) is critical but often overlooked
videos.creator_stance: Before moving to complex architectures, understand what's happening inside the network during training. Activation and gradient analysis is the diagnostic toolkit every practitioner needs.
notable_quotes: I would like us to have a very good intuitive understanding of the activations in the neural net during training

I imagine there's a more burning

about combing fluffy spheres like this.

videos.summary: Explores the Hairy Ball Theorem — the mathematical proof that you can't comb a hairy ball flat without creating at least one cowlick. Connects this to topology, wind patterns on Earth, and the Brouwer fixed-point theorem.
key_insights: You cannot comb a hairy ball without at least one point sticking up — this is a topological invariant

videos.summary: Deep visual explanation of what the Laplace transform actually means geometrically — not just how to use it, but what it's doing. Builds up a complex visualization showing how the transform maps functions into a new space.
key_insights: Most students learn to use Laplace transforms without understanding what they actually do — like driving without knowing how the engine works
The transform maps time-domain functions into the complex frequency domain, revealing exponential behavior
Building geometric intuition makes the transform feel natural rather than magical
videos.creator_stance: Math education should prioritize understanding over mechanical procedure. The Laplace transform is a perfect example where visual intuition transforms a mysterious tool into an obvious one.
notable_quotes: as a student, you can learn how to use it to solve equations and yet be left completely in the dark about what it's actually doing

videos.summary: Reviews DeepMind's AI system that invents fundamentally new scientific concepts — framing it as a landmark moment where AI moves from tool to genuine scientific contributor.
key_insights: The key question is whether AI can invent something fundamentally new — not just optimize existing ideas
DeepMind's system appears to generate genuinely novel scientific concepts, not just recombine existing ones
This represents a shift from AI as a tool to AI as a research partner
videos.creator_stance: If AI can genuinely invent new scientific concepts, this changes the nature of research itself. We're witnessing the beginning of AI as a co-scientist.

videos.summary: Humorous project building a 'mansplainer' AI that automatically corrects people in conversations. Uses it as a vehicle to explore AI personality, tone control, and the fine line between helpful and obnoxious AI behavior.
key_insights: Building an intentionally obnoxious AI reveals how much personality engineering matters in practical LLM applications
The line between 'helpful correction' and 'mansplaining' is a useful lens for understanding AI social dynamics
LLMs can be steered toward any personality axis — the challenge is choosing the right one
videos.creator_stance: Sometimes the best way to understand AI capabilities is through humor. Building a deliberately annoying AI teaches more about persona engineering than building a helpful one.
notable_quotes: Have you ever been in a situation where you're overhearing conversation and it dawns on you this person well intended is wrong

videos.summary: Analyzes the TiDAR paper from NVIDIA — a system that uses idle GPU capacity during autoregressive inference to run diffusion-based thinking, essentially doing background 'reasoning' while waiting for the next token.
key_insights: Autoregressive LLM inference is memory-bound, leaving GPU capacity unused — TiDAR exploits this gap
The system runs diffusion-based 'thinking' in the background during idle GPU cycles
This represents a paradigm shift: using inference-time compute for reasoning, not just generation
videos.creator_stance: This is clever engineering — instead of fighting the memory-bound nature of LLM inference, TiDAR turns it into an opportunity for background computation.
notable_quotes: it effectively makes good use of already observes that we don't have full GPU utilization during autoregressive large language model inference

videos.summary: Analyzes Google Research's Titans paper — an architecture that learns to memorize at test time, combining the benefits of transformers and memory-augmented networks for improved long-context handling.
key_insights: Titans introduces a memory module that learns during inference, not just during training
This addresses a fundamental limitation of transformers: fixed context windows
The architecture can adapt to new information without retraining — a form of continual learning
videos.creator_stance: Memory-augmented architectures like Titans represent the next evolution beyond pure transformers. The ability to learn at test time is a game-changer for long-context tasks.

videos.summary: Analyzes the Free Transformer paper — extending the decoder-based transformer with latent variables for underlying sequence decisions. Uses movie review generation as a motivating example.
key_insights: Adding latent variables to transformers allows models to make implicit decisions about sequence structure
The movie review example shows how the same movie can generate very different reviews based on latent 'quality' variable
This bridges the gap between deterministic generation and stochastic reasoning
videos.creator_stance: Latent variable models in transformers are underappreciated — they add a level of reasoning that pure autoregressive models lack.
notable_quotes: any given movie whether it's good or bad will have like good reviews and bad reviews

videos.summary: Response video to Theo (T3GGG) about MCP and Cloudflare's code mode. Argues that both the original article and the commentary miss a deeper insight about agent abstraction layers.
key_insights: The MCP debate isn't just about API design — it's about the right abstraction level for AI agent tool use
Cloudflare's code mode is interesting but may oversimplify the problem
The real question is whether agents should call tools directly or reason about tool capabilities first
videos.creator_stance: Technical debates about agent architecture matter because the abstractions we choose now will shape how AI agents evolve. Neither MCP nor code mode has it quite right.

videos.summary: Analyzes a paper proving theoretical limitations of embedding-based retrieval (vector databases/RAG). Shows there are fundamental limits to what can be retrieved using embeddings alone.
key_insights: There are proven theoretical limits to what embedding-based retrieval can capture — not just practical limitations
This has huge implications for RAG systems that rely on vector similarity search
Some queries fundamentally cannot be answered by embedding retrieval alone, regardless of model quality
videos.creator_stance: The RAG community needs to take theoretical limitations seriously. Vector databases aren't magic — there are provable boundaries on what they can do.
notable_quotes: the paper proves effectively that there are limitations to what can be retrieved

videos.summary: Analyzes the 'Context Rot' paper showing that LLM performance degrades as input context grows, even when models pass needle-in-a-haystack evaluations. Reveals a gap between benchmarks and real-world performance.
key_insights: LLMs that ace needle-in-a-haystack tests still degrade with real-world long contexts
The degradation is task-dependent — simple retrieval survives, complex reasoning doesn't
This paper exposes a fundamental gap between how we test and how we use long-context models
videos.creator_stance: Context rot is a critical finding — we've been overconfident about long-context capabilities because our benchmarks don't capture real-world degradation patterns.
notable_quotes: even though all of these models do these evaluations... the reality is that indeed as the task gets harder performance degrades

videos.summary: Analyzes the Energy-Based Transformers paper — combining energy-based models with transformers for a new learning paradigm that enables scalable language, video, and reasoning capabilities.
key_insights: Energy-based models provide a different lens for training transformers — optimizing energy landscapes rather than just likelihood
The approach scales to language modeling, video modeling, and reasoning tasks
Promising results on smaller-scale data suggest this paradigm could scale further
videos.creator_stance: Energy-based models have been underexplored in the transformer era. This paper shows they can be made practical and scalable.
notable_quotes: this paper combines the general concept of energy-based models with transformers and suggests a learning paradigm

videos.summary: Continues analysis of Anthropic's 'Biology of a Large Language Model' research — examining attribution graphs that reveal internal model circuits and how specific concepts are represented and processed.
key_insights: Attribution graphs reveal which internal circuits activate for specific concepts in LLMs
The 'replacement model' technique — training a cross-layer transcoder — makes model internals interpretable
This research is building a 'biology' of neural networks analogous to how we study biological brains
videos.creator_stance: Anthropic's interpretability work is among the most important research in AI. Understanding model internals isn't just academic — it's essential for safety.
notable_quotes: they are training a what they call a replacement model for the original transformer model

videos.summary: Reports on exclusive leaks about qualitative leaps in upcoming models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Covers OpenAI shutting down Sora to redirect compute, and Anthropic's renewed Pentagon interest.
key_insights: OpenAI shut down Sora to redirect compute toward their next frontier model (Spud)
Anthropic's Pentagon interest suggests military/government AI adoption is accelerating

videos.creator_stance: The competition between labs is driving them to make bold resource allocation decisions. The shift toward government/military AI use raises important ethical questions.
notable_quotes: For OpenAI, this has meant shutting down the Sora app to spare computing resources for the new Spud model

videos.summary: Explores the ethical implications of autonomous AI weapons and mass surveillance — examining the deadline day for government decisions on these technologies and the tension between security and privacy.
key_insights: Governments face a fundamental tension: autonomous weapons may be necessary for projecting power, but they remove human judgment from lethal decisions
Mass surveillance could reduce crime but at the cost of privacy — and people often accept what they think is inevitable
The deadline for these decisions is approaching faster than public debate can keep up
videos.creator_stance: These are civilization-level decisions that deserve public debate, not just military and intelligence community input. The 'inevitability' framing is dangerous.

transcript_segments.text: Okay, so clearly everyone's building
agents right now. And recently in
another video, I talked about the whole
sort of distinction between single user
agents and multi-user agents. And the
thing is, while people are building a
lot of single user agents for
themselves, almost nobody is thinking
about what actually happens when you
want to ship one of these multi-user
agents into production. And over the
past two years, I've seen so many
different things go wrong, both with my
own team, but with other people who I've
consulted and stuff like that. You see
things like API keys getting leaked. You
have things like rogue agents running up
like a 10k bill overnight. And then you
have even more weird things where
suddenly you realize that for one day
last week, your agents just kind of
hallucinated for 200 different users.
And while people are doing all these
amazing things with clawed code and open
claw and this is really having its
moment, if you're going to put something
actually into production that real world
users use, there are seven things that
you better make sure you've got locked
down before you put any agent into
production. And in this video, I'm going
to go through each one and talk about
the different things that you need to be
focused on. Now, to show these off, I
need an actual platform. And recently
I've been doing a number of things with
the guys from a startup called True
Foundry and they've agreed to sponsor
this. And one of the reasons I agreed to
this is that they actually have all
seven of these things in one place which
is actually rare even for a lot of the
hyperscalers. But here's the thing. Even
if you never use True Foundry, these
seven things apply to whatever system
you're building on. Think of them as
your checklist. So let's get into it.
Okay. So the first thing is model
control. You need a unified layer
between your code and your models. And
this is for a number of different
reasons. So first up, if you're building
any agentic system nowadays, you
probably don't just want to be using one
model. You want to be using a variety of
different models. And often that's even
going to be a variety of models from a
variety of different providers. While
Anthropics Claude models are fantastic
for things like tool calling and stuff
like that, they're not great perhaps at
multimodal and in that case maybe you
want to use Gemini. And then other times
you basically just need really sort of
simple calls. And if you realize that,
okay, we're going to be doing a lot of
those calls, you may even want to use
just an open model that you could
fine-tune to give you back a very
specific JSON output, etc. The other
thing too is you don't want to be hard
coding model names, especially with all
the labs updating their models almost
like monthly at the moment. You want to
be able to easily swap in and swap out
models and you really want to abstract
any API keys to one particular place
where you lock down the security.
Another thing that I'm seeing a lot that
relates to this is that the model
companies are deprecating models really
quickly. If you had something working
fantastic on claude 3.5 haiku and that
gets deprecated, you better have
something that you can swap in very
quickly. So in True Foundry here,
they're letting you connect up lots of
different model providers. But then
you've also got a playground where you
can actually test these out. This is
basically where we can look out to see,
are we getting the structured outputs
that we want? Are we needing to make
changes to the system prompt? All those
sorts of things. So, you want something
that easily lets you connect to all your
different models from different
providers and even nowadays be able to
quickly test open models with things
like Open Router. And of course, one of
the cool things that you can do here is
that not only can you select which
model, but you can select which region
you want it to be configured in. Now,
the second thing that you've really got
to lock down are your prompts. Your
prompts are your intellectual property,
right? If you're doing something for any
kind of LM app, the prompt is often what
makes the difference. And while models
are getting better at more generalized
prompts, if you're looking to do things
with structured outputs, which you
certainly should be, your prompts are
your IP. And you've got to stop thinking
about these as just being strings. In
many ways, you want to think of these as
being like a second tier of code. So,
you want to make sure that you version
them. You want to make sure that often
you don't even embed them into the code

key_insights: The gap between a working agent demo and a production agent is enormous — most teams underestimate it
Multi-user agents need cost controls, rate limiting, and graceful degradation that single-user agents don't
Monitoring agent behavior in production is harder than monitoring traditional software

videos.summary: Introduces Cracked Engineers — a tech jobs platform built by the creator to connect talented engineers with companies. Explains the motivation from founder requests for hiring help.
key_insights: The platform addresses a real pain point — founders repeatedly asking for help hiring talent
Community-driven job platforms can match culture fit better than generic job boards
Building products from community needs is the fastest path to product-market fit
videos.creator_stance: I built this because fellow founders kept asking me to help them hire. When you see the same request repeatedly, that's a product opportunity.
notable_quotes: I had a lot of fellow Founders basically asked me to help them hire talent

videos.summary: Interview with Imbue's head of infrastructure about training a 70B model from scratch at a small AI startup. Covers the engineering challenges and lessons learned.
key_insights: Small startups can train 70B models — but the infrastructure challenges are immense
Training at this scale requires solving distributed computing, data pipeline, and debugging problems simultaneously
The gap between running experiments and training production models is wider than most realize
videos.creator_stance: Training large models at a startup is a different beast than at a big lab. Imbue's experience shows it's possible but requires exceptional engineering.
notable_quotes: we are a pretty small AI startup

videos.summary: Deep dive into LLaMA 3 with Thomas Scialom from Meta — one of the key authors on LLaMA 2, Bloom, Toolformer, Code Llama, and Galactica. Covers architecture decisions, training data, and evaluation.
key_insights: LLaMA 3 represents Meta's most ambitious open model — with significant architectural improvements over LLaMA 2
Training data curation is as important as architecture — Meta invested heavily in data quality
The open model approach creates community feedback loops that proprietary models miss
videos.creator_stance: Thomas Scialom has been involved in every major Meta AI release. His perspective on LLaMA 3 development is uniquely valuable.
notable_quotes: he's been one of the authors on many impactful meta papers including Llama 2, Bloom, Toolformer, Code Llama, Galactica

videos.summary: Interview with Albert Gu and Karan Goel about State Space Models — covering their PhD work at Stanford, time at DeepMind, and the Cartesia AI startup building on SSM research.
key_insights: State Space Models offer a fundamentally different approach to sequence modeling — not attention-based
SSMs can be more efficient than transformers for long sequences, with comparable quality
Cartesia AI is commercializing SSM research, suggesting these models have real production potential
videos.creator_stance: SSMs are the most promising alternative to transformers I've covered. Albert Gu's work at Stanford could reshape how we think about sequence modeling.
notable_quotes: we started working on some of these SSM models

videos.summary: Interview with Unsloth AI's Daniel Han about making LLM fine-tuning 30x faster. Covers his background optimizing classical ML algorithms at NVIDIA and the technical approach behind Unsloth.
key_insights: Unsloth achieves 30x faster fine-tuning through kernel-level optimizations and memory management
Daniel Han's background at NVIDIA optimizing classical ML (t-SNE speedups of 1000x) informs the approach
Faster fine-tuning democratizes custom model training — making it accessible beyond big labs
videos.creator_stance: Daniel Han is one of the most practical AI engineers I know — his work at NVIDIA and now Unsloth directly translates to making AI more accessible.
notable_quotes: he worked at Nvidia for over a year where he was basically optimizing some of the classical ml algorithms

videos.summary: Interview with Hamel Husain — former GitHub engineer who worked on the precursor to GitHub Copilot, now an LLM consultant. Discusses building LLM applications in production.
key_insights: Hamel Husain was involved in what became GitHub Copilot — one of the earliest production LLM applications
Building LLM apps in production requires different skills than building prototypes
The consulting market for LLM applications is growing because most companies struggle with production deployment
videos.creator_stance: Hamel's experience building what became Copilot gives him unique insight into what works in production LLM applications.
notable_quotes: he was actually working on a project that was a precursor to the GitHub co-pilot

videos.summary: Interview with Julius AI founder Rahul — from Facebook/Uber engineer to building an AI data analysis tool with 500K users. Covers the journey from side project to production product.
key_insights: Julius AI grew to 500K users by solving a specific pain point — making data analysis accessible through natural language
The founder's journey from Facebook/Uber to startup shows the pull of AI product opportunities
Finding product-market fit in AI requires solving real problems, not just wrapping APIs
videos.creator_stance: Rahul's journey from big tech to AI startup is a pattern I see repeatedly. The opportunity in AI products is pulling talented engineers out of comfortable jobs.
notable_quotes: Rahul used to work after graduating he worked at Facebook for a couple of years then then Uber

transcript_segments.text: So, me and my team have been working on
this software product for about 6 months
when we came to the realization that we
needed a full rebuild, a new code base,
a new architecture, and we decided to
build out the core logic in a new
programming language, namely Rust. Now,
I have never written a single line of
Rust in my life before. I'm the Python
guy. That's what I do. That's what I've
been doing for 10 years. Rust is a
completely different world, and yet I
personally rebuilt the entire desktop
application in Rust in about 2 weeks. It
works. It runs way better than the
previous version. And the thing is, I
didn't write a single line of code
myself. AI wrote all of it. And you want
to know the funny or even ironic part to
this? The only time that I tried to
manually interfere with the code base, I
introduced bugs, like you always do when
you write code by hand. And that was the
moment I realized, "Okay, I am genuinely
past the point of writing code by hand
because it is just no longer the most
effective way to work for me." And if
you're being honest with yourself, you
are probably experiencing something
similar, right? The 30-minute code
tutorial that you used to watch now is a
single prompt. The document- ation or
guides that you would go through, you
would now plug them into Cloud Code with
the URL, and it would just do the work
for you. And I think a lot of developers
feel the same way, but don't yet fully
understand kind of like what to do with
this. So, in this video, I want to share
the five skills that I think actually
matter right now in the age of AI. And
this video is not going to be about how
to use Cloud Code or how to write better
prompts, but the deeper skills that will
keep you competitive as an engineer when
AI handles the implementation. So, for
over three decades, the implementation
of software was always the bottleneck,
turning ideas into functioning code.
That's why coding tutorials exist.
That's why you followed those boot
camps. That's why you spend years
mastering that language or that
framework because building was the hard
part. That bottleneck is now gone. And
when you remove that bottleneck,
something interesting happens because
all the stuff that used to be considered
soft skills or even responsibilities
just for senior engineers, things like
effective communication, critical
thinking, system design, architecture,
those suddenly become the actual hard
skills. The things that determine
whether you actually ship something
great or whether it falls apart. So,
here are the five skills that I think
matter most right now. All right, so the
first one is to think in building blocks
instead of lines of code. Now, what do I
mean with this? Well, you absolutely
don't need to understand your code base
at the line level anymore, but you still
need to understand it at the component
level. What are the building blocks of
your system? How do they connect? How is
data flowing from one block to another
one? And what happens if one of the
blocks fails? This is systems thinking,
is actually what made the Rust project
that I created possible. I didn't need
to know the Rust syntax. I needed to
understand the architecture of how data
is moving from the back end to the front
end, what components I need, and how to
wire them together. That understanding
is what I gave to AI, and then AI turned
it into a working code base. So, when I
say that I don't write code anymore, I
definitely don't mean that I am purely
five coding. I am very much involved in
the process, constantly reviewing it
from an architectural and a component
level because I know what good looks
like at the system level. So, if you
want to get better at this, I recommend
to read the book Designing
Data-Intensive Applications by Martin
Kleppmann. It's probably the most
recommended system design book out there
for a reason. And this book doesn't
teach you how to write code, but it will
teach you how to think about designing
systems. Things like data flows, failure
modes, trade-offs. That is the thinking
that you need. And now, practically,
before jumping into any project with AI,

videos.summary: Full-stack engineering tutorial on building your own AI operating system — critiquing the wave of 'claw' agent frameworks and proposing a more principled approach to agent architecture.
key_insights: The 'claw' frameworks (Open Claw, Nano Claw, etc.) are exciting but have architectural limitations
Building your own agent operating system gives you control over memory, tool use, and orchestration
A principled approach to agent architecture beats framework-hopping
videos.creator_stance: Everyone's excited about agent frameworks, but I think building your own AI operating system teaches you more and gives you better control.

videos.summary: Framework for understanding AI agent complexity — from simple LLM calls to multi-agent systems. Explains when each level is appropriate and when to avoid over-engineering.
specific_topics: LLM call vs workflow vs agent
key_insights: There are 5 distinct levels of AI agent complexity — from simple LLM calls to multi-agent systems
Most problems don't need full agent systems — simpler solutions are often better
Choosing the right complexity level is the most critical early decision in any AI project
videos.creator_stance: Before building an agent system, ask yourself: do I actually need one? Most problems are solved at levels 1-3, not level 5.
notable_quotes: one of the most critical things to get right in the beginning is deciding on the level of complexity that you need

key_insights: Pydantic is the backbone of reliable Python AI applications — validating inputs and outputs

key_insights: Human-in-the-loop should be added at strategic decision points — not everywhere

You can also always try to create these kind of like sub agents where one agent can be either made available to a system as a tool call and then subsequentially have tools underneath that or you could use the workflow approach where you just build a router and offload it to another LLM API call. These are all patterns that you can use in order to split it up but make it clear and don't make the problem and thus the context too large. And then the next one is memory. So this is the entire conversation, the message history going back and forth between the user and the assistant. And now this is a tricky one because this is often an area where you will not see any problems during development because you're running these short isolated examples with a couple of messages back and forth. But this is what users will start to complain about where they say, "Yeah, on turn 10 it completely forgot what we were talking about and it started to not follow my instructions anymore." So at all times you want to keep an eye on your message history and either prune it by simply like removing earlier instances within that message history or taking let's say the first 20 summarizing it and then putting that into the conversation. Again there are all kinds of tricks that you can do and again this will become apparent if you just look at literally the whole trace from system prompt to the entire user conversation. If you then look at that and you're like, damn, that's a lot of information, then that is probably a signal that the LLM also struggles with this. And then when it comes to prompts, we of course have the comprehensive instructions and domain knowledge. So this is really where you need to strike the balance between being specific enough, not being too vague, and not like overly engineering the prompt with if else statements with lots of cases. Uh, and especially you want to avoid the negative cases in there. So use few shot examples with positive examples of what the model should do. And if the prompt and the cases become too big, too large, break it up into another problem. And what's also very effective to manage this is that you use some type of state machine where you keep track of a state. And based on the state that the user is in, you have a different system prompt or a different at least a different part within the system prompt. So let's say you are uh walking the user through a flow whether it's an assessment an onboarding whatever and and then depending on where the user is within that journey you could have different instructions because if you capture the entire assessment in one big system prompt saying first we need to do that and if it's completed that we need to go to that phase those are generally signals that you want to break it up and just keep track of that state in a database and then during runtime on every message coming from a user, you just pull that context from the database and then get it into memory. That's where you engineer the message history. So in that sense, context engineering also doesn't have to be linear where you just look at the message history and just like prune it or summarize it whenever it gets too bloated. It can also mean that you keep track of a certain state and depending on that state, pull different system prompts. Maybe get rid of the message history entirely or build it up in such a way where you strategically implement certain messages at a certain point within the conversation history. And this can go back and forth or even in loops again like it really depends on the problem that you're solving in the application that you're building. This is what context engineering is about and it's very creative and the challenge is that it's often very hidden during the development process because the context builds up as you start to interact with the system. And that is something that a lot of engineers when they're working on the product are actually not doing and not used to because they are used to writing features, writing unit tests and then seeing that it passes. But the key to building effective AI systems is that it doesn't need to pass once. It doesn't need to pass twice, but it also needs to pass on turn 10 and also on turn 20. And that's where you get all of the complexities. All right, and that's it for this video. Thanks for watching. I hope you found it helpful. And if so, please leave a like and consider subscribing. If you are already a little bit more technical and have dabbled a little bit with building AI systems, then I recommend this video because that's where I go over all of the tools and libraries I use to build production AI systems. videos.summary: Deep dive into context engineering for AI agents — why agents fail in practice and how to design the context they receive. The gap between demo and production quality comes down to context design.
key_insights: Context engineering is more important than model selection for agent quality
Big companies struggle with AI products because of context design failures
Agents fail due to poor context engineering, not model limitations
videos.creator_stance: Context engineering is the most underrated skill in AI development.
notable_quotes: how hard it still is to get it right all the time in practice

Follow-along tutorials are the most effective way to learn agent development

videos.summary: 6-month check-in on AI video automation capabilities — testing how well current models can generate, edit, and automate video content creation. Tracks progress from previous benchmarks.
key_insights: AI video automation has improved significantly in 6 months but still requires human oversight
The gap between 'good enough for YouTube' and 'professional quality' is narrowing
Tracking capability progress over time reveals that improvements are exponential, not linear
videos.creator_stance: I test AI video automation every 6 months because the progress is real but often overstated in individual product launches.
notable_quotes: I basically do this every 6 months. How are the models kind of doing with video automation

videos.summary: Fireship covers CVE-2026-31431, a critical logic flaw in the Linux kernel present since 2017, exploitable via a 732-byte Python script. An AI scanning tool discovered the vulnerability, wrote the exploit, and designed a website for it. CrowdStrike confirmed active exploitation in the wild.
key_insights: A 100% reliable logic flaw existed in the Linux kernel since 2017 and was discovered by an AI tool
The exploit is only 732 bytes of Python and can be used with Metasploit for remote code execution
CISA added it to the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) list and CrowdStrike confirmed active exploitation
An AI system not only found the bug but wrote the exploit and designed a disclosure website autonomously
videos.creator_stance: Fireship treats this as a watershed moment for AI in security — AI can now find, exploit, and disclose vulnerabilities faster than humans, which is both impressive and concerning.
